children.text: Common Signs and Symptoms of Bipolar Disorder

Bipolar disorder can cause noticeable changes in mood, energy, sleep, activity, thinking, communication, judgment, and daily functioning. These changes occur during periods called mood episodes and are usually more intense, sustained, and disruptive than ordinary emotional ups and downs.

A person with bipolar disorder may experience manic episodes, hypomanic episodes, depressive episodes, or episodes with mixed features. Symptoms vary widely. One person may become highly energetic and euphoric, while another becomes intensely irritable, restless, or agitated. Depressive symptoms may involve sadness, but they can also appear as emotional numbness, exhaustion, withdrawal, hopelessness, or loss of interest.

The presence of one symptom does not mean that someone has bipolar disorder. Many symptoms associated with bipolar disorder can also occur with anxiety, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, trauma-related conditions, substance use, sleep deprivation, medical conditions, medication effects, or ordinary life stress.

What makes bipolar symptoms clinically important is the overall pattern: how many symptoms occur together, how long they last, how different they are from the person’s usual behavior, and how much they affect daily life.
Bipolar mood episodes involve significant changes in mood, energy, activity, concentration, and functioning that may continue for days or weeks and may be noticeable to other people.
This page focuses on common signs and symptoms. For a broader explanation of the condition, visit
Bipolar disorder is not identified through one isolated behavior.

A person may occasionally stay up late, feel excited, speak quickly, spend too much money, or become discouraged without having bipolar disorder. The concern becomes greater when several changes happen at the same time and represent a significant departure from the person’s usual functioning.
Healthcare professionals look at factors such as:
The number of symptoms occurring together
Whether symptoms occur most of the day
Whether similar episodes have happened before
The person’s usual sleep and energy pattern
Changes noticed by family members or close friends
The effect on work, school, relationships, finances, or safety
Medication, alcohol, cannabis, stimulant, and other substance use
Medical conditions that may contribute to the symptoms

During a mood episode, symptoms may affect several areas at once. For example, reduced sleep may occur together with increased energy, rapid speech, unusual confidence, impulsive spending, and irritability.
This combined pattern is more informative than reduced sleep alone.
Common Signs of a Manic Episode

Mania is a period of abnormally elevated, expansive, or irritable mood accompanied by increased energy or activity. Symptoms are severe enough to cause major impairment, require hospitalization, create serious safety concerns, or include psychotic symptoms in some cases.
Mania does not always look happy or cheerful. A person may appear excited and enthusiastic, but they may also become impatient, argumentative, agitated, hostile, or difficult to redirect.
Common manic symptoms include elevated or irritable mood, reduced need for sleep, racing thoughts, rapid speech, distractibility, exaggerated confidence, increased activity, and risky behavior.
A person experiencing mania may feel extremely happy, powerful, excited, or emotionally “high.”
The mood may appear out of proportion to the person’s situation. They may describe feeling better than ever, having unlimited potential, or being capable of accomplishing extraordinary things.
Excitement that is difficult to interrupt
A belief that failure is impossible
Feeling specially chosen, gifted, or important
The person may not recognize the mood as unusual because it feels positive from the inside.
Mania may present primarily as irritability rather than happiness.
Restless or unable to remain still

Family members may notice that ordinary conversations quickly become confrontational. A normally patient person may react strongly to minor inconveniences or view reasonable concerns as attempts to control them.
Irritability becomes more concerning when it appears alongside reduced sleep, increased energy, rapid speech, impulsivity, or unrealistic plans.
A reduced need for sleep is an important sign of mania or hypomania.

The person may sleep only two or three hours and still feel energetic, alert, and ready to continue working or socializing. They may say they no longer need much sleep or that resting would waste valuable time.

This differs from ordinary insomnia. Someone with insomnia usually wants to sleep and feels tired because they cannot. During an elevated bipolar episode, the person may sleep very little without initially feeling fatigued.
Staying awake most of the night
Beginning projects in the early morning hours
Cleaning, shopping, driving, or working while others are asleep
Sleeping briefly and waking with immediate energy
Becoming irritated when encouraged to rest
A major change in sleep combined with increased activity deserves prompt attention.
Mania can produce a strong drive to remain active.
Become involved in several new causes or organizations
Take on responsibilities beyond their available time or resources
Activity may increase without becoming more organized. The person may begin many tasks but finish very few because attention keeps shifting to new ideas.
Speech may become unusually fast, loud, continuous, or difficult to interrupt.
Talk for long periods without pausing
Move quickly from one subject to another
Feel an urgent need to express every idea
Become frustrated when others cannot follow
Send unusually long or frequent messages
Pressured speech may feel as though the words are being pushed out faster than the listener can process them.
A person experiencing mania may describe their mind as moving extremely fast.
Thoughts may seem to jump from one idea to another. The person may feel creative or mentally powerful, but the speed of thinking can make concentration and organized decision-making difficult.
“I have hundreds of ideas at once.”
“I cannot explain my thoughts quickly enough.”
“I need to act before the opportunity disappears.”
Racing thoughts can also occur with anxiety, stimulant use, sleep deprivation, and other conditions. Their meaning depends on the wider symptom pattern.
Attention may shift rapidly toward noises, people, messages, visual details, or new ideas.
For example, someone may begin discussing a work problem, notice a notification, start planning a trip, remember a business idea, and then abandon the original conversation.
Frustration from coworkers or family members
Confidence may become much stronger than the person’s abilities, experience, or circumstances reasonably support.
The person may believe they have exceptional talent, authority, wealth, influence, intelligence, spiritual power, or professional ability.
Examples may include believing that they can:
Solve a major scientific or social problem alone
Perform professionally in an unfamiliar field
In severe mania, grandiose beliefs may become delusional, meaning the person holds them firmly despite clear evidence that they are not true.
Mania can significantly affect judgment and awareness of consequences.
The person may believe the behavior is reasonable and may resist efforts to slow down or review the decision.
Some people experience a significant increase in sexual interest during mania or hypomania.
Making decisions that later cause regret or relationship conflict
Increased sexual behavior should be understood in the context of other mood and behavioral changes. It is not by itself proof of bipolar disorder.
During mania, a person may have difficulty recognizing that their behavior has changed or become unsafe.
They may feel healthier, more productive, or more capable than usual and may believe that other people are jealous, negative, controlling, or unable to understand their plans.
Poor insight can make it difficult to encourage evaluation. Family members may recognize the episode before the individual does.
Hypomania involves many of the same types of symptoms as mania, but the symptoms are less severe.

The change is still noticeable and different from the person’s usual behavior, but it does not cause the level of marked impairment associated with mania. Hypomania does not include psychosis and is not severe enough by itself to require hospitalization.
Hypomania can easily be missed because it may feel productive or enjoyable. The person may describe feeling energized, confident, social, creative, or highly motivated.
Feeling mentally sharper or more creative

Hypomania may appear beneficial at first, but the activity may become unsustainable. The person may overcommit, neglect routine responsibilities, create conflict, or make decisions that have consequences later.
Family members and close friends may notice the change even when the person believes nothing is wrong. Hypomanic periods may also be followed by depressive episodes.
A bipolar depressive episode may involve sadness, but depression can affect nearly every area of functioning.
The person may experience changes in mood, motivation, sleep, appetite, concentration, movement, energy, self-worth, and interest in daily life.
Bipolar depression can resemble major depressive disorder. This is one reason some people are initially treated for depression before previous hypomanic or manic symptoms are recognized.
A person may feel deeply sad, emotionally empty, discouraged, or unable to believe that circumstances can improve.
Not everyone appears tearful. Some people become quiet, irritable, emotionally distant, or unable to describe what they are feeling.
Activities that once felt enjoyable or meaningful may no longer provide satisfaction.
A person may lose interest in:
This loss of interest is sometimes called anhedonia.
The person may continue performing certain activities out of obligation but feel emotionally disconnected from them.
Depression may produce profound physical and mental exhaustion.
Ordinary activities may feel unusually demanding. Showering, preparing a meal, answering a message, or leaving the house may require significant effort.
Remain in bed for long periods
Avoid tasks because they seem overwhelming
Low energy is not necessarily laziness or lack of concern. It can be a significant symptom of depression.
Bipolar depression may involve sleeping too much, sleeping too little, or experiencing poor-quality sleep.
Remaining in bed without feeling rested
Sleep changes are most meaningful when they represent a clear difference from the person’s usual pattern.
A person may eat much less or much more than usual.
Eat only because someone reminds them
Lack the energy to shop or prepare meals
Appetite changes can also be caused by medical conditions, medication effects, stress, or other mental health concerns.
Depression can slow thinking and make ordinary decisions feel difficult.
Someone who usually works efficiently may spend hours trying to complete a simple assignment.
Feelings of Worthlessness or Excessive Guilt
The person may become highly critical of themselves and focus intensely on past mistakes.
They are failing at work or parenting
Other people would be better without them
These beliefs may not reflect the person’s actual circumstances, but they can feel completely convincing during depression.
Depression may lead someone to stop answering calls, cancel plans, avoid family members, or remain isolated.
Withdrawal may occur because the person:
Does not want to burden others
Has lost interest in social activity
Believes others do not want them around
Friends may interpret withdrawal as rejection when it is actually part of a depressive episode.
Some people move and speak more slowly. Others feel restless, unable to sit comfortably, or driven by internal agitation.
Remaining in one position for long periods
Repeatedly getting up and sitting down
Some people experiencing bipolar depression have thoughts about death, self-harm, or suicide.
Saying life is not worth living
Expressing that others would be better without them
Suddenly appearing calm after severe distress

Suicidal thoughts require serious attention. Call or text 988 in the United States for crisis support. Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room when there is immediate danger, a suicide attempt has occurred, or the person has a plan and access to means.
When to Seek Help for Bipolar Disorder
Signs of an Episode With Mixed Features
Bipolar symptoms do not always appear as a clearly separated emotional high or low.
An episode with mixed features includes symptoms associated with depression and symptoms associated with mania or hypomania during the same period.
A person may feel depressed, hopeless, or emotionally distressed while also experiencing:
For example, someone may feel worthless and hopeless while pacing, sleeping very little, speaking rapidly, and acting impulsively.

Mixed symptoms may be especially difficult to recognize because the person may appear energized without feeling happy. Depressive thoughts combined with agitation or impulsivity can create serious safety concerns.
The American Psychiatric Association recognizes that depressive and manic symptoms may occur together during episodes with mixed features.
Prompt professional evaluation is important when someone experiences severe depression together with agitation, racing thoughts, reduced sleep, or increased activity.
Some people experience psychosis during severe manic or depressive episodes.
Psychosis may involve hallucinations, delusions, severe paranoia, or difficulty distinguishing what is real.
Hearing voices other people do not hear
Seeing things other people do not see
Believing ordinary events contain special messages
Believing someone is watching or controlling them
Believing they have extraordinary powers or authority
Becoming intensely suspicious of trusted people
Speaking in a severely disorganized way
Acting on beliefs that place someone in danger

Psychotic symptoms may be consistent with the mood episode. During mania, a person may believe they possess extraordinary wealth, power, fame, or spiritual importance. During depression, they may believe they have committed an unforgivable act or caused a disaster.
Psychosis can also occur with other psychiatric, neurological, medical, medication-related, or substance-related conditions. It requires urgent professional assessment.
Severe mania may include hallucinations or delusions and can lead to unsafe decisions or hospitalization.
Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room when psychotic symptoms are accompanied by threats, dangerous behavior, severe confusion, inability to care for basic needs, or risk of harm.
Bipolar symptoms may be easier for family members, partners, friends, or coworkers to recognize because they can compare the person’s current behavior with their usual pattern.
A family member may say, “You do not seem like yourself,” before the individual recognizes the change.
Observations from trusted people can be helpful during an evaluation, particularly when mania or hypomania has affected insight.
How Symptoms Can Affect Daily Life
During an elevated episode, the person may appear highly productive but make disorganized or risky decisions. During depression, the person may struggle to begin basic tasks.

The effect may be different across settings. Someone may continue performing well at work while experiencing severe relationship or financial problems. Another person may maintain household routines but struggle internally with hopelessness and exhaustion.
Early Warning Signs of an Approaching Mood Episode
Some people notice recurring changes before a full mood episode develops.
Possible early warning signs of mania or hypomania include:
Possible early warning signs of depression include:
Early warning signs vary by person. A written mood plan may help identify the person’s usual pattern and clarify when to contact a healthcare professional.

Bipolar symptoms can occur in younger people, but evaluation can be complicated because normal development, attention difficulties, trauma, anxiety, substance use, sleep disruption, and family stress may produce overlapping behaviors.
Possible symptoms may include intense mood changes accompanied by significant changes in sleep, energy, activity, thoughts, or behavior.
Frequent temper outbursts alone do not establish bipolar disorder. The timing, duration, associated symptoms, developmental history, and level of impairment all matter.
Any child or teenager expressing suicidal thoughts, experiencing psychosis, or behaving dangerously needs immediate professional support.
Bipolar Disorder in Children and Teens for a focused discussion.
Symptoms That May Be Mistaken for Another Condition
Several conditions can cause symptoms that resemble bipolar disorder.
Both conditions may involve distractibility, rapid speech, restlessness, impulsivity, and difficulty completing tasks.
A key difference clinicians consider is whether symptoms are ongoing or occur in distinct episodes with changes in mood, sleep, energy, and functioning.
A person can also have both conditions.
Anxiety may cause racing thoughts, insomnia, restlessness, irritability, and difficulty concentrating.
In anxiety, the person may feel tired and distressed by the inability to sleep. During mania or hypomania, the person may need little sleep and still feel energized.
Trauma-related conditions may involve emotional reactivity, sleep problems, irritability, avoidance, impulsivity, and periods of intense distress.
A careful evaluation considers trauma history, triggers, episode duration, and associated changes in energy and activity.
Stimulants, cannabis, alcohol, recreational substances, medication effects, and withdrawal can influence sleep, mood, perception, energy, and judgment.
Accurate information about substance use helps clinicians determine whether symptoms represent a primary mood disorder, a substance-related condition, or both.
Thyroid disorders, neurological conditions, sleep disorders, hormonal changes, medication reactions, and other medical issues can affect mood and behavior.
Professional evaluation may include medical review or testing when clinically appropriate.
“Bipolar disorder means moods change every few minutes.”
Bipolar mood episodes usually involve sustained changes lasting days or longer. Brief emotional reactions may have many other explanations.
Mania may involve severe irritability, agitation, hostility, or aggression rather than euphoria.
Hypomania may initially increase productivity, but the activity may become disorganized, excessive, or unsustainable.
Depression may look like numbness, withdrawal, exhaustion, irritability, poor concentration, or loss of interest.
Diagnosis depends on the complete pattern, duration, severity, history, and effect on functioning.
“People always recognize their own manic symptoms.”
Mania may reduce insight. The person may believe they are functioning exceptionally well while others observe concerning changes.
“Everyone with bipolar disorder has the same symptoms.”
The type, severity, frequency, and combination of symptoms differ from one person to another.
Consider a professional psychiatric evaluation when mood, sleep, energy, thinking, or behavioral changes:
Continue for several days or longer
Are significantly different from the person’s usual behavior
Affect work, school, parenting, or relationships
Cause financial, legal, or occupational problems
Lead to unsafe driving, sexual behavior, or substance use
Cause family members to express serious concern
A person does not need to experience every symptom before seeking help.

Professional evaluation can help determine whether symptoms may be related to bipolar disorder, another mental health condition, medication or substance effects, sleep disruption, or a medical condition.

Call or text 988 in the United States for mental health or suicide crisis support. Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room when someone may harm themselves or another person, has attempted suicide, is experiencing dangerous psychosis, or cannot remain safe.

Professional evaluation can help determine whether a symptom pattern is consistent with bipolar disorder or whether another explanation should be considered. Treatment recommendations depend on the individual and may include psychiatric follow-up, therapy-informed support, medication management when clinically appropriate, or coordination with other healthcare professionals.
Telehealth appointments may be available for eligible patients physically located in Maryland, Washington DC, or Virginia when virtual care is clinically appropriate.

Common signs and symptoms of bipolar disorder include significant changes in mood, sleep, energy, activity, speech, thinking, concentration, confidence, judgment, and daily functioning.
Manic and hypomanic symptoms may include reduced need for sleep, increased energy, rapid speech, racing thoughts, distractibility, unusual confidence, irritability, impulsivity, and risky behavior.

Depressive symptoms may include persistent sadness or emptiness, loss of interest, fatigue, changes in sleep or appetite, difficulty concentrating, social withdrawal, feelings of worthlessness, and thoughts of death or suicide.
Some people experience depressive and elevated symptoms at the same time. Severe episodes may include psychosis.

No single symptom confirms bipolar disorder. What matters is the complete pattern, including duration, severity, recurrence, change from the person’s normal functioning, and effect on everyday life. A professional psychiatric evaluation can help clarify what the symptoms may mean and what kind of support may be appropriate.

children.text: How Bipolar Disorder Can Affect Daily Functioning

Bipolar disorder can affect a person’s ability to manage everyday responsibilities, make decisions, maintain routines, communicate effectively, and function consistently across different areas of life.

The impact may change depending on whether the person is experiencing mania, hypomania, depression, mixed symptoms, or a period of relative mood stability. Some people function well between episodes but experience significant disruption when symptoms return. Others continue to have concentration, sleep, motivation, or organizational difficulties after the most intense part of an episode has improved.

Daily functioning is not determined by mood alone. Changes in energy, judgment, attention, memory, impulse control, motivation, sleep, and insight may all influence how a person handles ordinary tasks.

A person may understand what needs to be done but struggle to complete it. Another person may become extremely active yet make poorly organized or unsafe decisions. Someone else may continue meeting responsibilities while using considerable effort to hide symptoms from others.

The effects of bipolar disorder vary. Difficulties in daily functioning do not mean a person is incapable, irresponsible, or unable to lead a meaningful life. They may indicate that symptoms are affecting practical abilities and that professional support should be considered.

This page focuses specifically on functional impairment: how bipolar disorder may influence a person’s ability to carry out everyday activities. For a broader discussion of its impact on work, relationships, finances, and home life, visit
Daily functioning refers to the ability to manage the tasks, decisions, routines, and responsibilities required in everyday life.
Getting out of bed and beginning the day
Recognizing when help may be needed
A person does not need to struggle in every area to experience meaningful impairment.

Someone may continue performing well at work while their home, finances, sleep, and relationships become increasingly disorganized. Another person may appear socially engaged but be unable to complete schoolwork or maintain personal care.
Daily functioning should therefore be evaluated across several areas rather than judged by one outward sign of success.
Functional Changes May Occur in Episodes
Bipolar disorder is generally episodic. A person’s ability to function may change substantially over time.

Before an episode, they may manage routines, responsibilities, and relationships consistently. During an episode, tasks that were previously manageable may become difficult, neglected, rushed, or unsafe.
After the episode improves, the person may need time to address:
This recovery period may continue even after the person’s mood appears more stable.
Functional improvement is therefore not always immediate. Someone may no longer be experiencing severe mania or depression but still need support rebuilding routines and responsibilities.
How Mania Can Affect Daily Functioning
Mania can significantly affect judgment, planning, self-awareness, attention, and impulse control.
The person may feel unusually capable and productive. However, increased activity does not always lead to effective functioning.
Start many tasks without completing them
Miss appointments because of competing plans
Become unable to follow structured routines

For example, a person may decide to start several businesses within one week, purchase equipment, contact potential clients, and make promises they cannot realistically fulfill. They may feel highly productive, yet ordinary responsibilities such as paying rent, attending work, or collecting children from school may be forgotten.
Mania may also affect a person’s ability to recognize impairment. They may believe their judgment is better than usual even when others observe serious changes.

Severe mania can make independent functioning unsafe. The person may require urgent evaluation when they cannot manage basic needs, are losing contact with reality, or are placing themselves or others at risk.
For a detailed explanation of elevated symptoms, visit
How Hypomania Can Affect Daily Functioning
Hypomania is less severe than mania, but it may still interfere with organized and sustainable functioning.
A person experiencing hypomania may appear energetic, confident, productive, and socially active. They may complete more work than usual or generate many new ideas.
However, difficulties may develop when the person:

A professional may begin several projects, agree to unrealistic deadlines, and respond to messages at all hours. Their output may initially increase, but accuracy, prioritization, and follow-through may decline.
A student may feel able to complete an entire semester’s work in a few days, yet submit rushed assignments or abandon tasks when a new idea becomes more interesting.
Hypomania may not cause obvious collapse in functioning. Instead, it may create subtle disruption, overcommitment, conflict, or consequences that become clear later.
How Bipolar Depression Can Affect Daily Functioning
Depression may reduce a person’s ability to begin, organize, and complete everyday activities.

The person may experience low energy, slowed thinking, poor concentration, reduced motivation, hopelessness, guilt, or loss of interest. These symptoms can make ordinary tasks feel physically and mentally demanding.
During bipolar depression, someone may struggle to:
A person may know that a task is important but feel unable to begin it.

For example, someone may receive a bill, understand that it needs to be paid, and still leave it unopened for several weeks because the process feels overwhelming. The problem is not a lack of knowledge. Depression may be affecting energy, concentration, decision-making, and task initiation.
Another person may remain in bed for most of the day while feeling guilty about unfinished responsibilities. That guilt may then make it even harder to act.
Bipolar depression may also affect speed. Reading, writing, speaking, movement, and decision-making may become slower than usual.
Some people experience depressive and elevated symptoms during the same period.
A person may feel hopeless, distressed, or emotionally low while also experiencing:
This combination can make daily functioning especially difficult.

The person may have enough energy to act but lack the emotional stability, judgment, or concentration needed to act safely. They may move quickly between tasks, arguments, worries, and impulsive decisions.
Higher safety concerns when suicidal thoughts are present
Prompt professional evaluation is important when agitation, impulsivity, reduced sleep, and depression occur together.
Mixed Features in Bipolar Disorder for a focused discussion
How Bipolar Disorder Can Affect Task Initiation
Task initiation is the ability to begin an activity without becoming stuck, distracted, or overwhelmed.
During depression, a person may have difficulty starting even simple tasks. They may spend a long time thinking about what needs to be done without taking the first step.
Remaining in bed despite planning to get up
Looking at laundry without beginning it
Delaying a phone call for several days
Opening a work document but being unable to write
Avoiding an appointment because getting ready feels too difficult
Leaving medication at the pharmacy because collecting it feels overwhelming
During mania or hypomania, task initiation may appear excessive rather than reduced. The person may begin many activities but struggle to choose which task deserves priority.
They may start cleaning, then move to online shopping, begin planning a trip, send several emails, and return to none of the original tasks.
In both cases, the difficulty involves organized action, although the outward behavior looks very different.
How Bipolar Disorder Can Affect Attention and Concentration
Concentration may be affected during both elevated and depressive episodes.
During mania or hypomania, attention may shift rapidly because the person is responding to multiple ideas, sensations, messages, and opportunities.
Abandon tasks when new ideas arise
During depression, concentration may feel slow or limited.
Take much longer to complete assignments
Avoid tasks that require sustained mental effort
Problems with concentration are not unique to bipolar disorder. They can also occur with anxiety, ADHD, trauma, medication effects, sleep deprivation, medical conditions, and substance use.
The timing and pattern of symptoms are important.
How Bipolar Disorder Can Affect Planning and Organization
Planning requires the ability to identify goals, arrange steps, estimate time, organize resources, and adjust when circumstances change.
Bipolar symptoms may interfere with one or more of these abilities.
During an elevated episode, a person may create overly ambitious plans without considering practical details.
During depression, planning may become difficult because every decision feels demanding.
A person may struggle to decide:
What to prepare for a meal
How to respond to an email
What time to leave for an appointment
How to divide a large project into smaller steps
This may lead to missed deadlines, unfinished responsibilities, clutter, and increased stress.
The resulting disorganization can then worsen shame, anxiety, and low mood.
How Bipolar Disorder Can Affect Memory
Some people report difficulty remembering information during or after mood episodes.
Forgetting why a task was started
During mania, memory difficulties may be related to rapid thinking, distractibility, limited sleep, and excessive activity.
During depression, slower information processing and reduced concentration may make it harder to absorb and recall information.

Medication, substance use, physical health conditions, stress, and sleep problems may also affect memory. Significant or worsening memory changes should be discussed with a qualified healthcare professional.
How Bipolar Disorder Can Affect Decision-Making
Decision-making involves evaluating options, considering consequences, and choosing an appropriate course of action.
During mania or hypomania, a person may make decisions quickly because they feel highly confident or believe opportunities must be acted on immediately.
Public statements that later cause regret
During depression, decision-making may become unusually slow.
The person may feel unable to choose between simple options or may avoid decisions entirely because they expect every outcome to be negative.
For example, someone may delay responding to an employer, paying a bill, choosing a treatment appointment, or asking for support because the decision feels overwhelming.
Both rushed and delayed decision-making can affect functioning.
How Bipolar Disorder Can Affect Time Management
Changes in energy, sleep, attention, and judgment may make it difficult to estimate and manage time.
During mania or hypomania, the person may schedule too many activities and assume they can complete them all.
Arrive late because they added extra tasks
During depression, the person may lose time while remaining inactive, sleeping, worrying, or attempting to begin a task.
A simple morning routine may take much longer than usual. The person may wake on time but still arrive late because dressing, eating, and leaving the house require significant effort.
Time-management difficulties can affect work, school, healthcare appointments, relationships, and family responsibilities.
How Bipolar Disorder Can Affect Communication
Communication may change across different mood states.
During mania or hypomania, the person may:
Assume others are disappointed in them
These changes may affect relationships with family members, coworkers, teachers, healthcare professionals, and friends.
Communication difficulties may also make it harder to ask for help at the time it is most needed.
How Bipolar Disorder Can Affect Self-Care
Self-care includes the routine activities required to maintain physical health, hygiene, nutrition, sleep, and medical care.
During mania, self-care may be neglected because the person feels too busy, does not believe rest is necessary, or is focused on new activities.
They may skip meals, remain awake for long periods, exercise excessively, or ignore symptoms of illness.
During depression, self-care may feel physically demanding. The person may stay in the same clothes, eat very little, rely on easily available foods, or postpone medical appointments.
Difficulty maintaining self-care can indicate that symptoms are becoming more severe.
How Bipolar Disorder Can Affect Household Management
Household functioning requires organization, planning, physical energy, and follow-through.
During mania or hypomania, someone may:
Cook or clean throughout the night
Neglect routine repairs while pursuing new ideas
During depression, someone may struggle to:
A disorganized home can increase stress and shame. The person may avoid visitors or feel unable to ask for practical help.
Support should focus on manageable tasks rather than criticism.
How Bipolar Disorder Can Affect Work Functioning
Bipolar disorder may affect reliability, productivity, communication, attendance, and judgment in the workplace.
During elevated mood, an employee may:
Produce a large amount of poorly organized work
Feel unable to manage ordinary pressure
Some people continue working while experiencing significant symptoms. Outward productivity does not always reflect internal stability.
Employment difficulties should be addressed through appropriate clinical, workplace, human resources, or legal channels depending on the situation.
Bipolar Disorder at Work for a detailed discussion
How Bipolar Disorder Can Affect School Functioning
Students may experience changes in attendance, concentration, motivation, organization, and academic performance.
During hypomania or mania, a student may:
Attend social events instead of sleeping
A sudden or recurring change in school performance may be one sign that professional assessment is needed, particularly when it occurs with major changes in sleep, energy, mood, or behavior.
How Bipolar Disorder Can Affect Financial Functioning
Managing money requires planning, impulse control, memory, and consistent attention.
During mania or hypomania, financial functioning may be affected by:
During depression, financial problems may develop because bills are left unopened, accounts are ignored, paperwork feels overwhelming, or the person lacks energy to resolve problems.
Financial consequences may continue long after the mood episode improves.

Safeguards may be helpful when they are agreed upon during a stable period. Examples may include transaction alerts, automatic payments for essential bills, spending limits, and consultation before major purchases.
How Bipolar Disorder Can Affect Parenting and Caregiving
Parenting and caregiving require consistency, patience, judgment, attention, and emotional availability.
During mania or hypomania, a parent may:
Make impulsive travel or school decisions
Become less aware of safety risks
During depression, a parent may struggle with:
Having bipolar disorder does not mean someone cannot be a capable parent. However, additional support may be needed during periods of impairment.
A practical family plan can identify trusted adults, transportation arrangements, childcare support, and steps to take when symptoms worsen.
How Bipolar Disorder Can Affect Social Functioning
Social functioning includes maintaining relationships, respecting boundaries, understanding social cues, and participating in communication.

During elevated mood, someone may become unusually social, intense, flirtatious, or demanding. They may contact many people, share private information, or become frustrated when others do not respond as expected.
During depression, the person may cancel plans, avoid messages, withdraw from friends, and feel disconnected from others.
Friends may view elevated social behavior as confidence and depressive withdrawal as rejection. The person may later feel embarrassed about what was said or done during an episode.
Social recovery may involve honest communication, appropriate accountability, and time to rebuild trust.
How Bipolar Disorder Can Affect Driving and Transportation
Safe driving requires concentration, judgment, impulse control, reaction time, and adequate sleep.
During mania or hypomania, a person may:
Become distracted by calls or ideas
During depression, fatigue, slowed thinking, reduced attention, or emotional distress may also affect driving.
Medication side effects, alcohol, cannabis, and other substances may create additional safety concerns.
Someone who feels too agitated, distracted, exhausted, impaired, or emotionally overwhelmed to drive should use safer transportation and contact an appropriate healthcare professional.
Some people return to their usual level of functioning between episodes. Others continue to experience difficulties even after the most severe mood symptoms improve.
These challenges may be described as residual symptoms or recovery-related difficulties.
A person may need support not only during an acute episode but also while rebuilding daily structure afterward.
Functional recovery can involve returning gradually to responsibilities, addressing practical consequences, and monitoring for early warning signs.
Some people work hard to hide their symptoms.
They may continue attending work, caring for children, or responding socially while experiencing substantial internal difficulty.
Spending most available energy on one area of life
Appearing productive at work but being unable to manage the home
Using multiple alarms and reminders to complete basic tasks
Sleeping very little to meet commitments
Feeling close to collapse while appearing outwardly calm
External success does not automatically mean that symptoms are mild.
A psychiatric evaluation should consider the effort required to maintain functioning, not only whether responsibilities are technically being completed.
A professional evaluation may examine how symptoms affect several areas of life.
What has changed from your usual routine?
Have you missed work or school?
Are you sleeping more or less?
Are others concerned about your behavior?
Have there been legal, financial, or safety consequences?
How long have these changes lasted?
The clinician may also ask about medication, substance use, medical conditions, trauma, sleep disorders, anxiety, ADHD, and other possible contributors.
Functional impairment is one part of diagnosis. It should be considered together with symptoms, duration, severity, and clinical history.
Practical Strategies That May Support Daily Functioning
Practical strategies do not replace professional care, but they may help reduce disorganization and make changes easier to recognize.
A basic routine may include consistent times for waking, meals, work, rest, medication, and sleep.
The routine should be realistic. An overly detailed schedule may become difficult to maintain.
Instead of “clean the home,” begin with “collect dishes from one room.”
Instead of “fix my finances,” begin with “open the latest bank statement.”
Smaller actions can reduce the sense of overload during depression and create clearer priorities during elevated mood.
Limit Major Decisions During Mood Changes
When possible, delay major purchases, travel, relationship decisions, job changes, and business commitments until they can be reviewed carefully.
A trusted person may help notice changes, review plans, provide transportation, or support appointment attendance.
The role and boundaries should ideally be discussed when the person is stable.
A sudden change in sleep or activity may be an early warning sign.
Tracking does not need to be complicated. A brief daily record of sleep hours, mood, energy, and major decisions may be useful.
During recovery, it may be necessary to reduce nonessential responsibilities and focus on basic needs.
Regular psychiatric care may help monitor symptoms, functioning, medication response, and emerging concerns.
Common Misconceptions About Functioning and Bipolar Disorder
“Someone who is working cannot be significantly affected.”
A person may maintain employment while struggling severely with sleep, finances, relationships, self-care, or internal distress.
“High productivity means the person is functioning well.”
Mania and hypomania may increase activity while reducing judgment, organization, and sustainability.
Depression may interfere with energy, concentration, planning, memory, and task initiation.
Some people hide difficulties or use considerable effort to maintain appearances.
“Stable mood means every problem immediately disappears.”
Practical, financial, occupational, and relationship consequences may continue after an episode improves.
Appropriate support can help preserve safety, autonomy, and long-term functioning.
Consider professional evaluation when changes in functioning:
Continue for several days or longer
Are significantly different from the person’s usual abilities
Lead to unpaid bills or unsafe spending
Cause household responsibilities to become unmanageable
Prevent adequate hygiene, meals, or medical care
Occur with reduced sleep, rapid speech, hopelessness, or risky behavior

Professional evaluation can help determine whether the changes may be related to bipolar disorder, another mental health condition, medication effects, substance use, sleep disruption, or a medical issue.
Immediate help is needed when someone may harm themselves or another person, experiences dangerous psychosis, cannot care for basic needs, or cannot remain safe.
Call or text 988 in the United States for crisis support. Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room when there is immediate danger.

Common Signs and Symptoms of Bipolar Disorder
Bipolar disorder can affect daily functioning by changing a person’s energy, sleep, attention, memory, judgment, motivation, communication, organization, and ability to complete responsibilities.

Mania and hypomania may increase activity while reducing planning, impulse control, and awareness of consequences. Bipolar depression may make it difficult to begin tasks, concentrate, make decisions, care for oneself, or maintain ordinary routines.

Functional impairment may affect work, school, finances, parenting, relationships, household management, transportation, and physical health. It may be visible to others, or the person may work hard to hide it.

Difficulty functioning does not define a person’s abilities or character. A professional psychiatric evaluation can help clarify the cause of the changes, determine how severely daily life is being affected, and identify appropriate next steps.

children.text: Bipolar disorder warning signs are changes that may suggest a manic, hypomanic, depressive, or mixed mood episode is beginning or becoming more severe. These changes can involve sleep, energy, activity, speech, concentration, judgment, behavior, relationships, and daily functioning.

Warning signs are not identical for every person. One individual may become unusually energetic and talkative before mania. Another may first become irritable, restless, or intensely focused on a new idea. Before depression, someone may begin withdrawing from others, sleeping more, losing interest in activities, or struggling to complete routine tasks.

A warning sign is also not the same as a diagnosis. Staying up late, feeling confident, becoming frustrated, or having a difficult week does not automatically mean someone has bipolar disorder. The concern increases when several changes occur together, continue over time, represent a noticeable departure from the person’s usual behavior, or begin affecting safety and everyday responsibilities.

Bipolar disorder can involve clear shifts in mood, energy, activity, concentration, and functioning. People may experience manic episodes, depressive episodes, or episodes containing both manic and depressive symptoms.

Recognizing warning signs early may create an opportunity to contact a healthcare professional, review current stressors and sleep patterns, involve trusted support, and address safety concerns before symptoms become more disruptive.
This page focuses specifically on warning signs. For a detailed description of established symptoms, visit
Common Signs and Symptoms of Bipolar Disorder.
What Is a Bipolar Disorder Warning Sign?
A bipolar disorder warning sign is a noticeable change that may occur before or during a mood episode.

Some warning signs are internal. The person may notice that their thoughts are moving faster, sleep feels unnecessary, ordinary activities no longer feel enjoyable, or simple decisions have become difficult.
Other warning signs are behavioral. Family members, friends, partners, teachers, or coworkers may observe changes such as:
Sleeping much less or much more
Showing unusual beliefs or severe suspicion
Warning signs matter most when they are considered as part of a pattern.

For example, one night of limited sleep after an important deadline may not indicate a mood episode. Sleeping only a few hours for several nights while remaining highly energetic, talking rapidly, spending impulsively, and beginning multiple projects is more concerning.
The most useful question is often not simply, “Is this behavior unusual?” It is:
Is this behavior significantly different from the person’s normal pattern, and is it occurring with other changes in mood, sleep, energy, judgment, or functioning?
Warning Signs May Be Different From Full Symptoms
An early warning sign may appear before a person meets the full clinical criteria for a mood episode.
For example, someone who has previously experienced mania may notice that they are:
Sleeping one or two hours less than usual
Checking social media throughout the night
Spending more time planning new projects
At that stage, the person may still be completing daily responsibilities. However, the combination may resemble the beginning of a previous episode.
Similarly, early depressive warning signs may include:
Taking longer to get out of bed
These changes may appear before depression becomes severe enough to prevent work, school, parenting, or personal care.
Recognizing a familiar pattern does not prove that an episode will develop. It can indicate that closer monitoring and communication with a healthcare professional may be appropriate.
Changes in Sleep as an Early Warning Sign
Sleep changes are among the most important warning signs to notice.
A person’s usual sleep pattern provides a useful baseline. A sudden or sustained change may deserve attention, particularly when it occurs with changes in mood, speech, activity, or behavior.
A reduced need for sleep can be associated with mania or hypomania.
The person may sleep only a few hours but wake feeling energized. They may believe that sleep is unnecessary or that resting would interfere with their plans.
Staying awake much later than usual
Waking after only a few hours
Working or cleaning throughout the night
Beginning projects while other people are sleeping
Feeling energetic despite several nights of limited sleep

A reduced need for sleep differs from insomnia. Someone with insomnia usually wants to sleep and feels fatigued because they cannot. During an elevated episode, the person may feel that very little sleep is enough.
Decreased need for sleep is a recognized feature of mania, especially when it occurs with increased speech, racing thoughts, distractibility, activity, or impulsive behavior.
Sleeping More or Remaining in Bed
Increased sleep may be an early warning sign of depression.
Struggle to wake in the morning
Feel exhausted despite sleeping for many hours
Some people experience insomnia during depression instead of increased sleep. They may wake repeatedly, rise very early, or feel unable to obtain restorative rest.
Dramatic changes in sleep can be a broader warning sign of mental health difficulties and should be considered alongside changes in mood, appetite, self-care, social engagement, and functioning.
Mania may begin gradually or become severe over a relatively short period. Early changes can appear positive because the person feels energized, confident, productive, creative, or socially engaged.
The warning signs become more concerning when activity increases while sleep, judgment, organization, and awareness of consequences decline.
A person may begin moving, working, exercising, socializing, or planning much more than usual.
Clean or reorganize the home overnight
Increased energy is not automatically mania. It becomes more meaningful when combined with a reduced need for sleep, rapid speech, unusual confidence, distractibility, or risk-taking.
A developing manic episode may change how a person communicates.
Sending frequent or unusually long messages
Becoming frustrated when others cannot follow
The person may feel a strong need to express every thought immediately.
Racing Thoughts and Increasing Mental Activity
The person may report that ideas are arriving too quickly or that their mind cannot slow down.
Acting quickly because an opportunity feels urgent
Racing thoughts can also occur with anxiety, stimulant use, sleep deprivation, and other conditions. The surrounding mood and behavioral pattern helps determine their clinical significance.
A noticeable increase in confidence may be an early warning sign when it is substantially different from the person’s usual personality.
The person may believe they can:
Complete an unrealistic amount of work
Persuade anyone to support an idea
Confidence may progress into grandiosity during more severe mania. Grandiosity involves an exaggerated belief in personal ability, importance, influence, wealth, knowledge, or power.
Some developing manic episodes appear as irritability rather than happiness.

Family members may initially interpret this as stress or a personality conflict. The pattern becomes more concerning when irritability appears with reduced sleep, increased activity, rapid speech, impulsivity, or unrealistic plans.
Using more alcohol or other substances
Making public statements without considering consequences
Risky or impulsive behavior is a recognized feature of mania, particularly when it represents a clear change from the person’s usual behavior.
A person approaching mania may begin abandoning routines that previously supported daily stability.
Going to bed at a regular time
The person may replace ordinary routines with new projects or social activities that feel more important.
Hypomania involves many of the same types of changes as mania, but it is less severe.

Because hypomania may feel pleasant or productive, warning signs can be overlooked. The person may believe they are simply feeling better, becoming more creative, or performing at their highest level.
Responding to messages at all hours
The main concern is not that the person feels good. It is that their mood, energy, sleep, and behavior have shifted noticeably from their usual baseline.
Hypomania may initially increase productivity. The person may complete work quickly, generate creative ideas, or participate more actively.
However, warning signs may appear when they:
Begin more projects than they can complete
Make commitments without reviewing existing obligations
Increased output is not always the same as stable functioning.
Friends, partners, or coworkers may notice that the person is unusually:
The person may not feel impaired. However, observations from people who know their usual behavior can provide important information.
Hypomanic Episodes for a focused explanation
Warning Signs of Developing Bipolar Depression
Bipolar depression may begin with subtle changes in interest, energy, sleep, concentration, and social engagement.
The person may not initially identify the experience as depression. They may describe feeling tired, disconnected, unmotivated, mentally slow, or unable to enjoy anything.
Withdrawal may occur because interaction feels exhausting or because the person believes they are a burden.
Activities that usually provide meaning or enjoyment may become less appealing.
The person may lose interest in:
Loss of interest or pleasure is a common depressive symptom and may appear before more obvious sadness.
The person may feel physically or mentally drained.
Taking longer to complete basic tasks
Spending more time sitting or lying down
A person may begin having trouble:
They may read the same information repeatedly without understanding or retaining it.
The person may become unusually focused on mistakes, failures, or perceived shortcomings.
These statements may be early indicators of worsening hopelessness or worthlessness.
Remaining in bed for long periods
A decline in personal care is a recognized warning sign that mental health symptoms may be interfering with daily functioning.
Changes in Work or School Performance
These functional changes may appear before the person openly discusses depression.
An episode with mixed features includes symptoms associated with depression and symptoms associated with mania or hypomania during the same period.
Feeling hopeless while having racing thoughts
Sleeping very little while feeling emotionally distressed
Having increased energy with severe irritability
Feeling mentally driven but unable to focus
Moving constantly while feeling emotionally low
Mixed presentations can be difficult to recognize because the person may not appear simply “high” or “low.”
A person may have the energy and impulsivity associated with an elevated state while also experiencing the hopelessness of depression. This combination may create significant safety concerns.
The American Psychiatric Association recognizes that people may experience manic and depressive symptoms at the same time during episodes with mixed features.
Prompt professional evaluation is important when severe agitation, reduced sleep, impulsivity, and depressive thinking occur together.
Behavioral Warning Signs Family Members May Notice
Family members may recognize a developing episode before the individual does.
Increased phone or social media activity
These signs are most useful when compared with the person’s normal functioning.

For example, frequent social activity may be normal for one person but a major change for someone who is usually reserved. Spending may be more concerning when it is uncharacteristic, unaffordable, and occurs with other elevated symptoms.
Bipolar warning signs may become visible through changes in workplace behavior.
Work difficulties do not confirm bipolar disorder. However, a clear change that occurs with mood, sleep, or energy symptoms may support the need for evaluation.
Warning Signs at School or College
Students may show warning signs through changes in attendance, activity, academic performance, and social behavior.
Making sudden educational or career plans
A change in academic performance is more clinically meaningful when it occurs alongside significant mood, sleep, energy, or behavioral changes.
Changes in money management may be among the first visible signs of an elevated episode.
During depression, warning signs may include:
Financial problems can continue after a mood episode has improved. Agreed safeguards established during stable periods may help reduce harm.
Changes in relationships may signal that a mood episode is developing.
Believing loved ones would be better without them
Avoiding conflict by disappearing or refusing to respond
Relationship difficulties have many possible causes. The concern increases when they occur as part of a broader mood and behavioral change.
Severe manic or depressive episodes may include psychotic symptoms.
Hearing voices others do not hear
Seeing things others do not see
Believing ordinary events contain special messages
Believing others are following or controlling them
Expressing unrealistic beliefs about extraordinary power, wealth, fame, or identity
Speaking in a severely disorganized way
Becoming unable to distinguish reality from personal beliefs
Acting on beliefs that create danger
Psychotic symptoms during severe mania may include disorganized thinking, delusions, or hallucinations.
Psychosis requires urgent professional evaluation because it may also be associated with substance use, neurological illness, medication effects, infection, or another psychiatric condition.
Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room when psychosis is accompanied by dangerous behavior, severe confusion, inability to care for basic needs, threats, or risk of harm.
Bipolar depression and mixed episodes may involve suicidal thoughts or behavior.
Discussing or developing a suicide plan
Saying there is no reason to live
Suddenly becoming calm after severe distress
Talking about suicide, making plans, expressing hopelessness, increasing substance use, withdrawing, and displaying extreme mood changes are recognized suicide warning signs.
Take suicide-related statements seriously. Do not assume the person is seeking attention or will simply feel better later.
Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room when:
The person has a specific plan
The person has access to lethal means
The person cannot agree to remain safe
Severe agitation, psychosis, intoxication, or impulsivity is present

Do not leave a person alone when there is an immediate risk of suicide. When it can be done safely, reduce access to firearms, large quantities of medication, and other potential means while emergency assistance is being arranged.
When to Seek Help for Bipolar Disorder.
Warning Signs After a Medication Change
Mood or behavioral changes may sometimes appear after a medication is started, stopped, missed, or adjusted.
Contact the prescribing professional when there is a noticeable increase in:
Do not abruptly stop, restart, increase, decrease, or combine psychiatric medications without guidance from the prescribing professional.

Emergency medical attention may be necessary for overdose, severe confusion, loss of consciousness, seizures, breathing difficulty, serious allergic reactions, or other potentially life-threatening symptoms.
Warning Signs Related to Alcohol or Substance Use
Changes in alcohol or substance use may occur before, during, or after a bipolar mood episode.
Making increasingly unsafe decisions while intoxicated
Substances may worsen mood symptoms, interfere with sleep, increase impulsivity, or produce symptoms that resemble mania, depression, anxiety, or psychosis.
A healthcare professional needs accurate information about alcohol, cannabis, stimulants, supplements, and other substances to make a careful clinical assessment.
Warning Signs During Pregnancy or After Childbirth
People with bipolar disorder or a history of serious mood episodes may need careful support during pregnancy and the postpartum period.
Urgent warning signs after childbirth may include:
Little or no sleep without fatigue
Thoughts of harming oneself or the baby

Postpartum psychosis is a medical emergency. Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room when a postpartum person becomes disconnected from reality, severely confused, dangerous, or unable to care safely for themselves or the baby.
Medication decisions during pregnancy or breastfeeding should be discussed with qualified healthcare professionals.
Warning Signs in Children and Teenagers

Bipolar disorder can occur in younger people, but careful evaluation is essential because development, ADHD, anxiety, trauma, sleep problems, substance use, and family stress may produce overlapping symptoms.
In children and teenagers, bipolar mood episodes can involve intense emotions and significant changes in sleep, activity, thoughts, or behavior that may continue for days or weeks.
Frequent temper outbursts alone do not establish bipolar disorder. A clinician must consider duration, associated symptoms, developmental history, context, and functional impact.
Any young person expressing suicidal thoughts, behaving dangerously, or experiencing psychosis needs immediate professional attention.
General warning signs can be helpful, but the most useful signs are often personal.

One person may consistently begin shopping online before mania. Another may start writing throughout the night. Someone else may become highly religious, intensely social, argumentative, or focused on a business idea.
Before depression, a person may stop listening to music, avoid cooking, begin missing morning appointments, or stop responding to one particular friend.
A personal warning-sign record may include:
Tracking is not intended to make someone monitor every ordinary emotion. It helps identify meaningful changes that resemble previous episodes.
What to Do When Warning Signs Appear
The appropriate response depends on the severity of the changes and the person’s individual care plan.
Contact an existing psychiatric provider when familiar warning signs return, sleep changes significantly, functioning begins to decline, or medication concerns develop.
A person who has not been evaluated may schedule a psychiatric assessment.
Sleep changes should be taken seriously. Reducing unnecessary late-night activity and discussing persistent sleep changes with a healthcare professional may be important.
Decisions can be reviewed when mood and judgment are more stable.
A trusted relative, partner, or friend may help notice changes, attend an appointment, provide transportation, or review major decisions.
The support person’s role should ideally be discussed during a stable period.
Alcohol and other substances may worsen mood instability, judgment, sleep, or medication-related concerns. A healthcare professional can provide individualized guidance.
Medication changes should only be made with appropriate clinical guidance.
Common Misconceptions About Bipolar Warning Signs
“A warning sign guarantees that an episode will happen.”
A warning sign indicates a possible change. It does not predict the future with certainty.
“Warning signs are the same for everyone.”
Some patterns are common, but personal warning signs vary.
“Feeling happy or energetic is always a warning sign.”
Normal happiness, motivation, and productivity are not bipolar episodes. The concern is a substantial change in mood, sleep, energy, behavior, and functioning.
Some episodes begin with irritability, agitation, insomnia, or conflict.
“Only the person experiencing symptoms can identify warning signs.”
Family members and close friends may recognize changes before the person does, especially when insight is affected.
“A person must wait until symptoms are severe before contacting a provider.”
Early contact may help address concerns before functioning or safety deteriorates.
“Every difficult behavior is caused by bipolar disorder.”
People with bipolar disorder still experience ordinary emotions, disagreements, habits, and personality traits. Behavior should be considered within the larger clinical pattern.
Consider professional evaluation when warning signs:
Represent a major change from usual behavior
Affect sleep, work, school, or relationships
Lead to unusual spending or risk-taking
Cause family members to express concern
Include unusual beliefs, hallucinations, or confusion

Contact an existing provider promptly when early signs of a previous episode return, medication has been stopped or missed, sleep decreases significantly, depression worsens, or daily functioning begins to decline.
Immediate emergency help is needed when someone may harm themselves or another person, experiences dangerous psychosis, cannot care for basic needs, or cannot remain safe.
Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room during an immediate mental health emergency.

How Bipolar Disorder Can Affect Daily Functioning
Bipolar disorder warning signs are changes in sleep, mood, energy, speech, thinking, activity, judgment, behavior, or daily functioning that may signal the beginning or worsening of a mood episode.

Possible warning signs of mania or hypomania include needing less sleep, becoming unusually energetic, talking rapidly, developing many plans, increasing spending, showing unusual confidence, becoming more irritable, and taking greater risks.

Possible warning signs of depression include withdrawal, loss of interest, fatigue, changes in sleep or appetite, difficulty concentrating, declining self-care, reduced functioning, hopelessness, and suicidal thoughts.
Warning signs are most meaningful when several occur together, represent a clear change from the person’s normal behavior, resemble a previous episode, or begin interfering with daily life.

Recognizing warning signs early does not guarantee that an episode can be prevented. It may provide an opportunity to contact a healthcare professional, involve trusted support, protect sleep and finances, and address safety concerns before symptoms become more severe.
